Prosecutors Allege $2.5 Billion Super Micro Server Diversion to China

Sun entered the plea Thursday in U.S. District Court in Manhattan. He admitted to four charges: conspiring to violate U.S. export controls, smuggling, defrauding the U.S. government and obstructing justice, Reuters reported, citing a court filing.
In March, prosecutors charged Sun and two others tied to Super Micro with conspiring to divert about $2.5 billion in U.S. AI servers to China, according to the indictment.
The scheme began around 2024 and involved shipping servers without required licenses, it said.

The indictment described Sun as a broker and fixer. It alleged that he helped set up fake servers in December 2025 and lied to a U.S. Department of Commerce official during an inspection. According to the indictment, the servers had already been diverted to China.

The U.S. restricts sales of advanced AI chips to China on national security grounds. According to the indictment, those restrictions cover Nvidia’s B200, H100 and H200 graphics processing units, as well as servers equipped with these chips.

The California-based AI-server maker said it terminated Sun and cut ties with the other defendants earlier this year.
Super Micro Computer has a market capitalization of $27.50 billion, a 52-week high of $58.51 and a 52-week low of $19.49.
